items.prompt: In L1, what happened to the defect rate when QA took two weeks of leave?
choices: It rose sharply, from 3% to 15%
It stayed about the same
It fell, since engineers took over
items.explanation: In the illustrative scenario nothing else changed, so the jump exposed how much the team had leaned on one person.

items.prompt: What does 'externalizing quality' mean?
choices: Hiring an outside firm to write and maintain all of the tests
Publishing test results for customers to read
Responsibility for correctness drifts to a downstream gate
items.explanation: The author stops treating correctness as theirs because a gate exists after them.

items.prompt: A moral hazard is when the person taking a risk is not the one who ...
choices: reviews the work afterwards
pays if it goes wrong
wrote the first version
items.explanation: The author can cheaply prevent the bug but QA bears the cost of finding it.

items.prompt: Why did engineers on L1's team write shallow tests?
choices: The system made moving on locally rational
They had never been taught how to write tests
Management told them tests were optional
items.explanation: It was an incentive effect, not a skill or character flaw.

items.prompt: Which describes quality in a team with shared ownership?
choices: A responsibility held by exactly one named specialist
Something checked only once, right before release
A property of the merged code, owned by its author
items.explanation: Shared ownership puts the responsibility back on whoever writes the change.

items.prompt: Which scenario shows the same shape as a moral hazard?
choices: A runner trains harder before a race
A driver with full insurance takes more risks
A cook tastes the soup several times while seasoning it
items.explanation: Being protected from a loss changes how much risk someone takes.

items.prompt: What was the one variable that changed in L1's scenario?
choices: Whether QA was present
The code review process
The release cadence
items.explanation: That is why the scenario isolates the dependence on one person.

items.prompt: Is the defect jump in L1 best explained by careless engineers?
choices: Yes, they stopped caring once QA left
Yes, review standards fell during the leave
No, the incentive structure explains it
items.explanation: The same careful people behaved rationally under the incentives the system gave them.

items.prompt: A team's defect rate stays flat when its QA engineer is away, but jumps when its most senior reviewer is away. What does this most directly suggest?
choices: Quality is already shared evenly across all of the authors on the whole team
The QA engineer's role is redundant and should be removed outright
The senior reviewer is the real downstream safety net the team leans on
Engineers become more careful whenever the QA engineer is absent
items.explanation: The gate people lean on is whoever's absence moves the numbers, regardless of job title. It is the dependence, not the role name, that signals externalized quality.
items.reference:
Where the catching happens
with a QA-only gate: authors lean on one downstream person
with shared ownership: authors catch their own mistakes first
absence test: does the defect rate move when one person leaves?
Why: a downstream gate makes thin tests locally rational, so the system, not the people, is what externalizes quality.
items.learnMore:
Externalizing quality and moral hazard

When the person best placed to prevent a bug is not the one who pays for it, they rationally spend less effort on it. A QA gate creates that gap without anyone intending it.

Common mistake

Blaming individual engineers for carelessness instead of looking at what the system rewards.
items.reflection: Think of a review or approval step in your own work. Does its existence make anyone upstream a little less careful?

items.prompt: An author skips an edge-case test because a manual pass follows. QA misses it and it reaches production. Who bore the cost of the author's shortcut at each stage?
choices: Nobody at write time; QA and users later
The author, immediately, through a failing local test
The whole team equally, at the moment of the merge
Only QA, since users never see the escaped defect
items.explanation: That gap between who saves the effort and who pays is the moral hazard. The author saved twenty minutes and others absorbed the consequence.

Caring has no relationship to the quality of a written test
QA must approve every request about test practices first
The incentive that made thin tests rational is unchanged

choices: The one where authors write tests and QA explores beyond them
The one where authors merge thin tests expecting QA to catch gaps

items.explanation: Having QA is not the problem. The habit of treating QA as the only net is. A team with QA as a complement has not externalized.

items.prompt: Treating testing strategy as an architectural decision means it is ...
choices: left to each engineer's own personal habits and preferences
chosen deliberately, written down, and revisited
set once and never changed again
items.explanation: The three marks are deliberate, visible, and revisited.

items.prompt: Who should own unit tests for new logic in the strategy table?
choices: The author, inside the same PR
A separate team after release
Only the QA engineer
items.explanation: Putting the owner at the author keeps cost and prevention together.

items.prompt: Which layer catches a service breaking its agreement with a consumer?
choices: Unit tests
Manual exploratory testing
Contract tests
items.explanation: Contract tests exist for exactly the boundary between services.

items.prompt: In the strategy table, what is manual QA's new job?
choices: The single remaining gate before every release
Exploratory judgment on top of automation
Writing and maintaining every unit test
items.explanation: It shifts from sole net to complement.

items.prompt: Why write the strategy down?
choices: So anyone can check who owns a layer
So QA can be removed from the team
So tests never need to change
items.explanation: Visibility makes ownership answerable instead of assumed.

items.prompt: Where does an accidental testing strategy usually come from?
choices: A formal vote taken by the whole team in a meeting
A requirement from customers
Early patterns copied by later contributors
items.explanation: It accretes: one module sets a pattern and others copy it.

items.prompt: Which end-to-end set does the table favor?
choices: As many as the team can possibly write
A small curated set with an owner
None, since they are slow
items.explanation: Quality over count, and someone responsible for them.

items.prompt: Should a written strategy be reviewed again later?
choices: Yes, as the system grows
No, once written it is final
Only if QA asks for it
items.explanation: A strategy that never changes fossilizes.

items.prompt: Nobody on a team can say who owns end-to-end tests, and several fail intermittently. Which fix matches the idea of strategy as a decision?
choices: Name an owner and a small curated set in the written table
Ask all engineers to keep an eye on the failures informally
Delete the end-to-end layer and rely on manual testing
Add more end-to-end tests to cover the failing flows
items.explanation: The gap is a missing decision, not missing tests. A named owner and a small set make the layer answerable and maintainable.
items.reference:
A decided strategy answers three things
what is tested at which layer (unit, contract, end-to-end)
who owns each layer, by name or team
where it is written, and when it is revisited
Why: an undecided strategy accretes by copying, so risk concentrates in whoever happens to pay attention.
items.learnMore:
Testing strategy as an architectural decision

Treat 'what is tested, at what level, by whom' like a service boundary: chosen deliberately, written where anyone can read it, and reviewed as the system grows.

Common mistake

Writing the table once and never revisiting it, so it fossilizes into the next accidental default.
items.reflection: Pick one system you work on. Can you name who owns each layer of its tests, and where that is written?

items.prompt: A strategy table was written two years ago and the team has since split into six services. What is its main risk now?
choices: It is too long and detailed for new engineers to read through
It makes QA's manual pass unnecessary everywhere
It forces every service to use identical tests
It has fossilized and may no longer describe real ownership
items.explanation: Writing it down is not enough. Without revisiting, the table drifts from the system it claims to describe.

Manual QA pass: the only gate, blocking, owned by one person
Contract tests: owned by the producing team, blocking on merge
End-to-end: curated set, shared owner, blocking
items.explanation: Any layer owned by one person as the sole net recreates the dependence from L1, no matter how the table is formatted.

items.prompt: A colleague says 'we have lots of tests, so we have a testing strategy'. What is missing for it to count as a decision?
choices: More unit tests than integration tests overall
A higher overall coverage percentage on the main branch
A deliberate, written choice of layers and owners
A dedicated QA engineer attending planning sessions
items.explanation: Tests existing is not the same as having decided what is tested where and by whom. The decision is the artifact.

items.prompt: Which lever works even if nobody changes voluntarily?
choices: Leading by example
A team-wide announcement
A blocking CI gate
items.explanation: A required check applies to every PR automatically.

items.prompt: What happens to a test left red for days with no owner?
choices: It becomes more trusted over time
It teaches that red does not matter
It gets fixed by the gate itself
items.explanation: Unowned failures erode the gate's credibility.

items.prompt: What does 'leading by example' mean here?
choices: Writing thorough tests for your own hardest code
Telling everyone else exactly how they ought to test
Reviewing only other people's tests
items.explanation: Skipping tests on your own gnarly change undoes your message.

items.prompt: How should an escaped regression be treated?
choices: As a quiet fix with no follow-up
As a reason to blame the author
As a short real incident review
items.explanation: A retro asks what in the strategy let it through.

items.prompt: Why is a blocking gate the path of least resistance?
choices: It is optional but encouraged
Passing is the only way to merge
It runs only on weekends
items.explanation: No one has to remember or agree; the constraint holds by default.

items.prompt: Which lever depends most on others noticing over many months?
choices: Leading by example
The blocking gate
A required status check
items.explanation: Example compounds socially, slowly.

items.prompt: Telling people to care more about quality usually ...
choices: always works within a week
works only for new hires
rarely works on its own
items.explanation: Slogans leave the incentives untouched.

items.prompt: The quarantine idea from test-suite-architecture helps the gate by ...
choices: removing all flaky tests silently
keeping triage fast and visible
making tests optional
items.explanation: Visible ownership with a deadline protects trust in red.

items.prompt: A team announces 'quality is everyone's job' in an all-hands but changes nothing else. Six weeks later behavior is unchanged. Which lever was missing?
choices: A longer announcement with more concrete examples
A second all-hands repeating the same message every month
A written apology from leadership for past defects
A blocking gate that makes the constraint mechanical
items.explanation: Announcements need to be backed by structure. The gate changes what the path of least resistance is, whether or not anyone is persuaded.
items.reference:
Four levers without authority
1. blocking gate: mechanical, works on day one
2. fast, visible triage of broken tests
3. leading by example on the hardest code
4. regressions treated as real incidents
Why: only the gate works if nobody else changes voluntarily; the other three compound as others follow.
items.learnMore:
Levers without authority

Instructions rarely move habits; changing what the path of least resistance rewards does. The blocking gate is mechanical, so it is usually pulled first and makes the other levers easier.

Common mistake

Announcing 'quality is everyone's job' and expecting behavior to change without any structural change.
items.reflection: Where in your own work could a mechanical constraint replace a request people have to remember?

items.prompt: A suite has had three tests red for a week and engineers merge anyway after re-running. Which lever addresses the cause?
choices: Leading by example on the hardest code of each sprint cycle
Fast, visible ownership of every red test with a due date
Running the suite more often during working hours
Adding a manual check before each merge instead
items.explanation: The credibility of the gate is what is eroding. Assigning owners and dates restores the meaning of red.

The blocking gate; the merge button stays enabled

items.explanation: Silence signals the gate is not really trusted. A short retro on what in the strategy let it through is the lever.

items.prompt: What was Marcus's objection really about?
choices: Zero ramp-up on one service under one deadline
A principled opposition to the idea of writing tests at all
A dislike of CI tools
items.explanation: The disagreement was narrower than it sounded.

items.prompt: How long was the exception for the payments service?
choices: Forever
Six months
Two weeks
items.explanation: A short, dated window keeps it from becoming permanent.

items.prompt: Where was the exception recorded?
choices: In a private chat with Marcus
In the strategy document, visible to all
Nowhere, to avoid confusion
items.explanation: Visibility keeps it from being a hidden favor.

items.prompt: What did Priya do to cut the ramp-up cost?
choices: Paired to write a first contract test as a template
Wrote every one of the missing tests alone, overnight
Disabled the contract suite
items.explanation: A template removes the from-scratch cost under deadline.

items.prompt: Why not simply override Marcus?
choices: He held formal authority over Priya's performance review
Overrides are forbidden by CI
It would make the next proposal harder to land
items.explanation: Steamrolling a valid concern costs future trust.

items.prompt: What should happen when the exception's end date arrives?
choices: The exception renews automatically
The gate applies fully again
The team votes to drop the rule
items.explanation: A closing date is what keeps the rule credible.

items.prompt: Which kind of rule stays credible longer?
choices: One with a visible, tracked exception path
One with no exceptions whatsoever, for anyone, ever
One with silent, unlimited exceptions
items.explanation: Rigid rules get routed around; silent ones decay.

items.prompt: Is Marcus's worry treated as simple resistance to change?
choices: Yes, it is dismissed politely as mere resistance
Yes, it is escalated to management
No, it is treated as a real, specific cost
items.explanation: The story shows a correct objection being engaged.

items.prompt: A second team asks for the same exception 'until things calm down', with no date. Compared with Marcus's case, what is missing?
choices: A formal vote from every engineer on the team
An end date, an owner, and a plan to remove the cost
A promise that no other team will ever ask for one later
A statement that the gate is unimportant here
items.explanation: Without those, the exception can never close and trust in the gate erodes, as the assumed model in the demo shows.
items.reference:
A tracked exception has four parts
a named owner
an end date
written where everyone sees it
a plan that removes the cost (e.g. a template test)
Why: a visible, dated exception lets a rule bend without breaking; an open-ended one teaches the gate is optional.
items.learnMore:
Negotiating instead of overriding

A correct objection usually narrows to one service under one deadline. A time-boxed, written exception with a ramp-up plan keeps the mechanism intact while paying the real cost.

Common mistake

Granting a quiet exception in chat with no date, so it never closes and the rule quietly becomes optional.
items.reflection: Recall a rule at work that someone made an exception to. Was the exception visible and dated, or quiet and open-ended?

items.prompt: Marcus's exception expires in two weeks but the contract tests are still unwritten. What best preserves the rule's credibility?
choices: Quietly extend it so the deadline is not affected further
Remove the contract requirement from the table for everyone
Make the overrun visible and decide it explicitly, not silently extend
Ask Priya to merge the PRs on the team's behalf
items.explanation: A silent extension is how exceptions become permanent. An explicit, recorded decision keeps the date meaningful.

Nothing, since the director's decision settles it completely
The director is asked to justify it in a private channel
The gate is disabled until the director is satisfied
items.explanation: Authority changes who can decide, not why visibility matters. A hidden exception from a director teaches the same lesson as any quiet one.

Recording the exception in the shared strategy document

items.explanation: Treating a valid concern as resistance signals that objections are not heard, which makes the next one harder to land.

items.prompt: What kind of bug reached production in week 6?
choices: A total outage of the CI system lasting an entire day
A null-handling edge case in an untested branch
A typo in the documentation
items.explanation: It lived in a path no test covered.

items.prompt: How long was the retro Priya proposed?
choices: About 30 minutes
A full two-day workshop
Two minutes in chat
items.explanation: Proportionate to the bug's size.

items.prompt: What single question drove the retro?
choices: Who wrote this code?
Why was QA not here?
What about the strategy let this through?
items.explanation: It focuses on the system, not the person.

items.prompt: What concrete change came out of the retro?
choices: A rule banning every edge case from the codebase
A new table row for null and boundary paths
Dismissing the author as a lasting consequence
items.explanation: The strategy table was updated.

items.prompt: What would a quiet fix have taught the team?
choices: That gaps past the gate cost nothing
That the gate is perfect
That retros are too long
items.explanation: Silence signals no consequence.

items.prompt: Retros for regressions should be ...
choices: Identical to a full outage review
Skipped when the fix is easy
Scaled to the size of the problem
items.explanation: Proportionate keeps them sustainable.

items.prompt: Which doc was updated after the incident?
choices: The employee handbook
The testing strategy table
The release notes only
items.explanation: The learning goes back into the decided strategy.

items.prompt: The retro treats the regression as ...
choices: A real incident worth the team's attention
An embarrassing secret to be kept inside the team
A routine non-event
items.explanation: That is the fourth lever from L2.

items.prompt: After a small escaped bug, a team spends two hours blaming the author. Compared with Priya's retro, what went wrong?
choices: It was far too short to find anything useful or lasting
It involved too few people from outside the team
It targets a person instead of what the strategy missed
It produced a change to the testing strategy table
items.explanation: The retro asks what in the strategy let the bug through. Blame teaches people to hide gaps, not close them.
items.reference:
Week 6: the short retro
30 minutes, scaled to the size of the bug
one question: what in the strategy let this through?
output: a changed table, e.g. a new row for null-handling paths
Why: a quiet fix teaches that gaps past the gate cost nothing; a short real retro keeps the gate meaningful.
items.learnMore:
Regressions as short incidents

A rare bug that slips past the gate is the cheapest moment to learn what the strategy misses. A brief retro that changes the table is proportionate and keeps the signal honest.

Common mistake

Holding a long, blame-focused post-mortem for a small bug, or skipping the review entirely.
items.reflection: Think of the last small bug you fixed quietly. What would a thirty-minute look at why it got through have changed?

items.prompt: A regression is traced to an untested boundary path. Which output best completes the retro?
choices: A new, owned row in the strategy table for that path
A promise from the author to test more carefully
A longer release checklist that QA reviews every time
A note in chat that the bug is now fixed
items.explanation: A durable change to the decided strategy outlasts any individual's promise.

items.prompt: Why is a regression 'worth 30 minutes' when the fix itself is quick?

items.explanation: The fix repairs one bug; the retro repairs the signal that gaps matter.
items.reference:
Week 6: the short retro
30 minutes, scaled to the size of the bug
one question: what in the strategy let this through?
output: a changed table, e.g. a new row for null-handling paths
Why: a quiet fix teaches that gaps past the gate cost nothing; a short real retro keeps the gate meaningful.
items.learnMore:
Regressions as short incidents

A rare bug that slips past the gate is the cheapest moment to learn what the strategy misses. A brief retro that changes the table is proportionate and keeps the signal honest.

Common mistake

Holding a long, blame-focused post-mortem for a small bug, or skipping the review entirely.
items.reflection: Think of the last small bug you fixed quietly. What would a thirty-minute look at why it got through have changed?

items.prompt: Six months after launch, regressions are always fixed quietly. What is the likely effect on the gate's credibility?
choices: It strengthens since fewer meetings are held
It slowly erodes as gaps appear costless
It stays unchanged because the suite still runs
It is replaced by QA's manual pass entirely
items.explanation: Credibility rests on perceived consequence. Silence removes it even while the mechanical check keeps running.
